The observation that only around 10 to 20% of evaluated samples have non-zero density and contribute to the final image motivated acceleration methods that localize the surface interface [S1].

The claim states that the observation that only 10-20% of samples have non-zero density motivated acceleration methods that localize the surface interface. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'As observed by Piala et al. [PC21] and Hu et al. [HLC∗ 22], only around 10 to 20% of the evaluated samples have non-zero density and actually contribute to the final image. To address this, acceleration methods aim to localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in these relevant regions...' This directly confirms both the statistic and the causal link to the motivation for localization methods.
supported

The general workflow involves: (1) learning implicit functions over an initial voxel grid to produce a coarse approximation of scene geometry [S1]; (2) progressively pruning empty voxels during training based on this initial geometry signal [S1]; and (3) using hierarchical structures or sparse grids to cull unused features from dense grids, improving efficiency when the surface of interest is known or can be progressively refined [S2].

The claim accurately reflects the information provided in the sources. Source [S1] explicitly states that methods 'learn implicit functions over an initial voxel grid to produce a coarse approximation of scene geometry' and then 'progressively prune empty voxels during training based on this initial geometry signal.' Source [S2] confirms that when the surface is known, structures like octrees or sparse grids 'can be used to cull away the unused features in the dense grid,' and notes that in NeRF settings, this involves progressive refinement. The claim synthesizes these points correctly.
supported
By refining the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface, these methods significantly reduce the number of required MLP evaluations, thereby improving computational efficiency [S1].

The claim states that refining sampling strategies to focus on the localized surface reduces MLP evaluations and improves computational efficiency. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'By refining the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface, these methods significantly reduce the number of required MLP evaluations, thereby improving computational efficiency.' It further explains that methods use sparse data structures to 'localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in these relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space,' which leads to 'rendering speedups of up to 10 times.' Thus, every part of the claim is directly supported by the text.
supported
Sparse voxel grids allow skipping empty regions during ray tracing, leading to rendering speedups of up to 10 times compared to standard NeRF [S1].

The claim states that sparse voxel grids allow skipping empty regions during ray tracing, leading to rendering speedups of up to 10 times compared to standard NeRF. Source [S1] explicitly contains the sentence: 'The use of a sparse voxel grid allows the renderer to skip empty regions during tracing a ray, leading to rendering speedups of up to 10 times compared to the standard NeRF implementation.' This directly supports every part of the claim.
supported

The core challenge in applying sparse structures to NeRF is that surfaces emerge during training, so space-partitioning data structures cannot be precomputed in advance and must be periodically updated [S1, S2].

The claim states that surfaces emerge during training, preventing precomputation of space-partitioning data structures and requiring periodic updates. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Surfaces typically emerge during training, so space-partitioning data structures cannot be precomputed in advance and must be periodically updated.' Source [S2] corroborates this by stating: 'in the NeRF setting, surfaces only emerge during training... this leads to a more complex training process in which the sparse data structure must be periodically updated.' Both sources fully support every fact in the claim.
supported

Early approaches like NSVF [LGZL∗ 20] and Efficient-NeRF [HLC∗ 22] introduced multistage coarse-to-fine strategies using sparse grids or two-level octrees (NerfTree) to dynamically adapt voxelization to the underlying scene structure [S1, S2].

The claim states that NSVF [LGZL* 20] and Efficient-NeRF [HLC* 22] introduced multistage coarse-to-fine strategies using sparse grids or two-level octrees (NerfTree) to dynamically adapt voxelization. Source [S1] explicitly confirms that TNSVF [LGZL* 20] adopts a multistage, coarse-to-fine strategy using sparse grids. It also confirms that Efficient-NeRF [HLC* 22] builds a two-level octree (NerfTree) and uses a coarse-to-fine approach. Both sources confirm that these methods dynamically adapt the structure (pruning/refining) because surfaces emerge during training. All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

This family of methods uses sparse data structures (sparse grids, octrees, VDBs) to localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space to reduce MLP evaluations [S1].

The claim states that the family of methods uses sparse data structures (specifically mentioning sparse grids, octrees, and VDBs) to localize the surface interface, concentrate samples in relevant regions, skip empty space, and reduce MLP evaluations. Source [S1] explicitly confirms all these points: it lists sparse grids, octrees, and VDBs as examples of sparse data structures used to localize the surface and eliminate empty voxel cells; it states this ensures neural fields are only evaluated in non-empty regions (reducing evaluations); and it mentions that sparse voxel grids allow skipping empty regions during ray tracing.
supported
Later works incorporated VDB structures [YLMM23] to further optimize traversal and memory usage [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that VDBs [YLMM23] are used to localize the surface and eliminate empty voxel cells, which ensures neural fields are only evaluated in non-empty regions. This process effectively skips empty space, thereby reducing MLP evaluations and improving computational efficiency (optimizing traversal and memory usage).

To address this, methods typically adopt a multistage, coarse-to-fine strategy where regions are progressively refined and pruned as necessary [S1, S2].

The claim states that methods adopt a multistage, coarse-to-fine strategy where regions are progressively refined and pruned. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that 'TNSVF ... and several other works ... adopt a multistage, coarse-to-fine strategy in which regions are progressively refined and pruned as necessary.' Source [S2] similarly states that 'NSVF ... and several concurrent works ... adopt a multistage, coarse to fine strategy in which regions of the feature grid are progressively refined and culled away as necessary.' Both sources confirm the specific strategy and actions described in the claim.
